title: What refresh() does, in the order it does it
summary: The twelve steps of AbstractApplicationContext.refresh, and the two places in it that explain most startup bugs: post-processors run in phases, and bean instantiation is nearly the last thing to happen.
entry: Put a breakpoint on the first line of AbstractApplicationContext.refresh and step over each numbered call. The comments in that method are the table of contents for this path.

steps.notice: Read the numbered comments before anything else. Twelve calls, in a synchronized block, and every startup question you have is answered by which of them runs first.

Three passes, not one: BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessors that are PriorityOrdered, then Ordered, then the rest, and only then plain BeanFactoryPostProcessors. Anything instantiated in here is built before a single BeanPostProcessor exists.
The one that turns your @Configuration classes into bean definitions, follows @Import and @ComponentScan, and evaluates @Conditional. All of Boot's auto-configuration arrives through here.
Registration only - the BeanPostProcessors themselves are instantiated here, which is why they cannot post-process each other or anything created earlier.
Where your beans are finally built, one at a time, in definition order. The last line is the SmartInitializingSingleton callback: everything exists, nothing has started yet.
Lifecycle beans are started, and only then is ContextRefreshedEvent published. A listener on that event can assume every SmartLifecycle is already running.
Note the filter: only SmartLifecycle beans with isAutoStartup() are started. A plain Lifecycle bean sits there doing nothing until somebody calls context.start().
Shutdown, and the order is deliberate: ContextClosedEvent first, so listeners still have a working context, then lifecycle stop, then destroy callbacks.

Reverse phase order, and each phase waits up to timeoutPerShutdownPhase for its stop(Runnable) callbacks. A SmartLifecycle that overrides stop(Runnable) and never calls the callback adds thirty seconds to every shutdown.
